notes: Sense and Sensibility is primarily a voice-driven novel. Austen's narrator is omnisciently ironic, and the most signature material is often NOT the famous plot moments but rather the sustained satirical digressions on character, social behavior, and self-deception. Key signature types include: (1) the famous opening inheritance plot with ironic narration of John Dashwood's moral decline; (2) character-defining sketches delivered through free indirect discourse; (3) Marianne/Elinor contrast passages that carry interpretive weight for critical debates about sense vs. sensibility; (4) dialogue scenes of social comedy (Palmers, Steeles, Mrs. Jennings); (5) Willoughby's confession scene; (6) the climactic revelation of Lucy's marriage to Robert. Downstream should hunt especially for ironic narratorial asides embedded in chapter middles, the free indirect discourse passages where a character's self-justification is exposed by the prose's own logic, and the sustained comic set-pieces that establish Austen's register.

examples.passage_hint: The family of Dashwood had long been settled in Sussex. Their estate was large, and their residence was at Norland Park, in the centre of their property
examples.why: The novel's famous opening; establishes the inheritance world and sets the ironic tone that governs everything that follows.

examples.passage_hint: an imperfect articulation, an earnest desire of having his own way, many cunning tricks, and a great deal of noise, as to outweigh all the value of all the attention which, for years, he had received from his niece and her daughters
examples.why: Ironic set-piece on the great-uncle's favoritism toward the child; the rhetorical escalation ('all the value of all') is signature Austen style.

examples.passage_hint: He was not an ill-disposed young man, unless to be rather cold hearted and rather selfish is to be ill-disposed: but he was, in general, well respected
examples.why: Paradigmatic Austen ironic understatement; widely cited in criticism as defining her technique of moral evaluation through apparent qualification.

examples.passage_hint: people always live for ever when there is an annuity to be paid them; and she is very stout and healthy, and hardly forty. An annuity is a very serious business; it comes over and over every year
examples.why: Mrs. John Dashwood's reasoning about annuities is a sustained comic voice passage; the repetition 'comes over and over every year' captures her comic self-interest perfectly.

examples.passage_hint: it was very well known that no affection was ever supposed to exist between the children of any man by different marriages; and why was he to ruin himself, and their poor little Harry
examples.why: The gradual reduction of the promise to nothing is one of the most famous comic-ironic sequences in English fiction; this passage marks the key rhetorical move.

examples.passage_hint: Elinor, this eldest daughter, whose advice was so effectual, possessed a strength of understanding, and coolness of judgment, which qualified her, though only nineteen, to be the counsellor of her mother
examples.why: The foundational character definition of Elinor; critical debates about Austen's endorsement of 'sense' over 'sensibility' begin here.

examples.passage_hint: Marianne's abilities were, in many respects, quite equal to Elinor's. She was sensible and clever; but eager in everything: her sorrows, her joys, could have no moderation. She was generous, amiable, interesting: she was everything but prudent.
examples.why: The paired introduction of Marianne establishes the novel's central thematic opposition; the final clause is one of Austen's most economical ironies.

examples.passage_hint: It was enough for her that he appeared to be amiable, that he loved her daughter, and that Elinor returned the partiality. It was contrary to every doctrine of hers that difference of fortune should keep any couple asunder
examples.why: Mrs. Dashwood's romantic doctrine rendered in free indirect discourse; the irony is that her 'doctrine' is precisely what will cause suffering.

examples.passage_hint: Esteem him! Like him! Cold-hearted Elinor! Oh! worse than cold-hearted! Ashamed of being otherwise. Use those words again, and I will leave the room this moment.
examples.why: Marianne's explosion at Elinor's measured language; critically central to the novel's interrogation of whether emotional restraint is virtue or repression.

examples.passage_hint: Dear, dear Norland! said Marianne, as she wandered alone before the house, on the last evening of their being there; when shall I cease to regret you!—when learn to feel a home elsewhere!
examples.why: Marianne's apostrophe to Norland is a set-piece of sensibility rhetoric; the exclamatory, address-to-landscape style is deliberately rendered susceptible to ironic reading.

examples.passage_hint: Lady Middleton seemed to be roused to enjoyment only by the entrance of her four noisy children after dinner, who pulled her about, tore her clothes, and put an end to every kind of discourse except what related to themselves.
examples.why: Signature Austen satirical portrait; the devastating economy of 'put an end to every kind of discourse' defines Lady Middleton in one clause.

examples.passage_hint: Sir John was a sportsman, Lady Middleton a mother. He hunted and shot, and she humoured her children; and these were their only resources.
examples.why: The parallel structure and the word 'resources' do ironic double work; signature Austen compression of social critique.

examples.passage_hint: A woman of seven and twenty, said Marianne, after pausing a moment, can never hope to feel or inspire affection again
examples.why: Marianne's pronouncement on women of twenty-seven is widely quoted as illustrating her romantic absolutism; ironic given the novel's resolution.

examples.passage_hint: She was perfectly disposed to make every allowance for the colonel's advanced state of life which humanity required.
examples.why: Free indirect discourse rendering Marianne's condescension as apparent generosity; a miniature of Austen's ironic technique.

examples.passage_hint: His name was good, his residence was in their favourite village, and she soon found out that of all manly dresses a shooting-jacket was the most becoming.
examples.why: Ironic enumeration of Marianne's reasons for admiring Willoughby; the bathetic climax ('shooting-jacket') is signature Austen comedy.

examples.passage_hint: Their taste was strikingly alike. The same books, the same passages were idolized by each—or if any difference appeared, any objection arose, it lasted no longer than till the force of her arguments and the brightness of her eyes could be displayed.
examples.why: The qualification clause ('the force of her arguments and the brightness of her eyes') is a perfect Austen ironic deflation of romantic intellectual compatibility.

examples.passage_hint: In Colonel Brandon alone, of all her new acquaintance, did Elinor find a person who could in any degree claim the respect of abilities, excite the interest of friendship, or give pleasure as a companion.
examples.why: Establishes the Elinor-Brandon parallel and signals the novel's eventual pairing logic; interpretively important for readings of the double marriage plot.

examples.passage_hint: Brandon is just the kind of man, said Willoughby one day, when they were talking of him together, whom every body speaks well of, and nobody cares about; whom all are delighted to see, and nobody remembers to talk to.
examples.why: Willoughby's witty dismissal of Brandon is one of his most memorable speeches; the rhetorical chiasmus defines both speaker and subject.

examples.passage_hint: There are some people who cannot bear a party of pleasure. Brandon is one of them. He was afraid of catching cold I dare say, and invented this trick for getting out of it. I would lay fifty guineas the letter was of his own writing.
examples.why: Willoughby's cruel flippancy about Brandon's urgent departure; dramatic irony since the reader later learns Brandon was summoned by Eliza's distress.

examples.passage_hint: We have been engaged these four years. Four years! Yes.
examples.why: Lucy Steele's revelation of her engagement to Edward; the staccato exchange is among the most dramatically compressed moments in the novel.

examples.passage_hint: Lucy was naturally clever; her remarks were often just and amusing; and as a companion for half an hour Elinor frequently found her agreeable; but her powers had received no aid from education
examples.why: Elinor's assessment of Lucy is the novel's most extended study of the difference between natural cleverness and educated refinement; critical to the novel's class and gender themes.

examples.passage_hint: The business of self-command she settled very easily;—with strong affections it was impossible, with calm ones it could have no merit.
examples.why: Marianne's dismissal of Elinor's self-command is rendered in free indirect discourse; the irony is that it perfectly predicts Marianne's own eventual transformation.

examples.passage_hint: It is so ridiculous! When is a man to be safe from such wit, if age and infirmity will not protect him?
examples.why: Marianne's rhetorical question about Colonel Brandon's age; the word 'infirmity' for a man of thirty-five is a fine example of her comic absolutism.

examples.passage_hint: Sir John wanted the whole family to walk to the Park directly and look at his guests. Benevolent, philanthropic man! It was painful to him even to keep a third cousin to himself.
examples.why: The mock-heroic salutation 'Benevolent, philanthropic man!' is signature Austenian ironic excess; establishes her technique of satirical apostrophe.

examples.passage_hint: The youthful infatuation of nineteen would naturally blind him to every thing but her beauty and good nature; but the four succeeding years—years, which if rationally spent, give such improvement to the understanding, must have opened his eyes to her defects of education
examples.why: Elinor's extended reflection on Edward's engagement is a sustained piece of self-protective reasoning; the parenthetical on 'rationally spent years' is a quietly devastating aside.

examples.passage_hint: Happy, happy Elinor, you cannot have an idea of what I suffer. Do you call me happy, Marianne? Ah! if you knew!—And can you believe me to be so, while I see you so wretched!
examples.why: The key dramatic irony scene; Marianne assumes Elinor has no suffering while Elinor conceals her own. Critically central to the novel's argument about concealed versus expressed feeling.

examples.passage_hint: MY DEAR MADAM, I have just had the honour of receiving your letter, for which I beg to return my sincere acknowledgments. I am much concerned to find there was anything in my behaviour last night that did not meet your approbation
examples.why: Willoughby's letter is one of the novel's most formally ironic documents; the cold bureaucratic courtesy ('sincere acknowledgments') in a letter that destroys Marianne.

examples.passage_hint: Like half the rest of the world, if more than half there be that are clever and good, Marianne, with excellent abilities and an excellent disposition, was neither reasonable nor candid.
examples.why: The narrator's generalizing aside on self-deception is one of the most quoted pieces of Austenian moral commentary in the novel.

examples.passage_hint: Lord! thinks she to herself, they are all so fond of Lucy, to be sure they will make no difficulty about it; and so, away she went to your sister, who was sitting all alone at her carpet-work, little suspecting what was to come
examples.why: Mrs. Jennings's breathless account of Anne Steele's revelation is a comic set-piece; the colloquial rush of the narration is signature Austen free indirect report.

examples.passage_hint: Elinor's office was a painful one.—She was going to remove what she really believed to be her sister's chief consolation,—to give such particulars of Edward as she feared would ruin him for ever in her good opinion
examples.why: The narrator's summary of Elinor's position before telling Marianne about Edward; the phrase 'chief consolation' is cruelly ironic given what Elinor herself has endured.

examples.passage_hint: Four months!—Have you known of this four months? Elinor confirmed it. What! while attending me in all my misery, has this been on your heart? And I have reproached you for being happy!
examples.why: Marianne's recognition of Elinor's concealed suffering is the emotional climax of the sense/sensibility theme; widely discussed in criticism.

examples.passage_hint: She felt all the force of that comparison; but not as her sister had hoped, to urge her to exertion now; she felt it with all the pain of continual self-reproach, regretted most bitterly that she had never exerted herself before; but it brought only the torture of penitence, without the hope of amendment.
examples.why: The narrator's description of Marianne's penitence is a psychologically precise passage; the phrase 'torture of penitence without the hope of amendment' is a memorable formulation.

examples.passage_hint: Tell me honestly a deeper glow overspreading his cheeks, do you think me most a knave or a fool?
examples.why: Willoughby's self-interrogating question to Elinor opens his confession scene; one of the most dramatically unexpected moments in the novel.

examples.passage_hint: The world had made him extravagant and vain—Extravagance and vanity had made him cold-hearted and selfish. Vanity, while seeking its own guilty triumph at the expense of another, had involved him in a real attachment
examples.why: The narrator's moral anatomy of Willoughby is the most sustained piece of psychological-social analysis in the novel; critical to readings of Austen's social determinism.

examples.passage_hint: She felt that his influence over her mind was heightened by circumstances which ought not in reason to have weight; by that person of uncommon attraction, that open, affectionate, and lively manner which it was no merit to possess
examples.why: Elinor's self-aware reflection on Willoughby's continued hold over her mind is a rare moment of the narrator exposing Elinor's vulnerability; interpretively significant.

examples.passage_hint: She rushed to the drawing-room,—she entered it,—and saw only Willoughby.
examples.why: One of the most effective chapter-ending shocks in Austen; the triple rhythm of the sentence enacts the reader's own surprise.

examples.passage_hint: Elinor could sit it no longer. She almost ran out of the room, and as soon as the door was closed, burst into tears of joy, which at first she thought would never cease.
examples.why: Elinor's emotional release on learning Lucy married Robert is one of the most satisfying moments of the novel; the restraint of the surrounding chapters makes this eruption all the more powerful.

examples.passage_hint: His heart was now open to Elinor, all its weaknesses, all its errors confessed, and his first boyish attachment to Lucy treated with all the philosophic dignity of twenty-four.
examples.why: The ironic final clause ('philosophic dignity of twenty-four') is quintessential Austen; it simultaneously validates Edward and gently deflates his self-importance.

examples.passage_hint: Marianne Dashwood was born to an extraordinary fate. She was born to discover the falsehood of her own opinions, and to counteract, by her conduct, her most favourite maxims.
examples.why: The narrator's summation of Marianne's fate is the most critically discussed passage in the novel's conclusion; the ironic distance between 'extraordinary fate' and the conventional marriage plot it describes.

examples.passage_hint: The whole of Lucy's behaviour in the affair, and the prosperity which crowned it, therefore, may be held forth as a most encouraging instance of what an earnest, an unceasing attention to self-interest, however its progress may be apparently obstructed, will do
examples.why: The narrator's ironic moral drawn from Lucy's success is one of Austen's most sardonic set-pieces; the mock-didactic framing is signature.
